speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
The purpose of the bill is to give to the Exchequer Court of Canada jurisdiction to deal with divorce actions in the case of persons residing in Quebec and Newfoundland. Jurisdiction as to alimony, care of children and other matrimonial causes will remain in the provincial courts of those two provinces.
This bill does not establish divorce courts in Quebec or Newfoundland, or interfere in any way with provincial rights. It does not change the grounds for divorce. It does not make available to persons residing in Quebec or Newfoundland anything not now available to them, but merely transfers the hearing of divorce petitions filed by persons residing in those two provinces from parliament to the Exchequer Court of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to make any particular comment on this course of action, except to say it is becoming so prevalent as to amount to the following of a precedent. Many people seem to feel that parliament has some control over expenditures, but the experience of the last several years has been that the control is more theoretical than actual. Within the last few months we have granted power to the government, in advance of any accounting, to expend tens of millions, and have ratified expenditure about which we know nothing.
Just before I came into the chamber I secured a copy of Durell's Parliamentary Grants, for the purpose of referring to the days when things were otherwise. It is still the authority as to the responsibility of the executive to the House of Commons, but it is more honoured in the breach than in the observance. At page 20 I find these words:
The proper office of parliament, as Mill points out,-
The author is quoting John Stuart Mill.
-is "to watch and control the government, to throw the light of publicity on its acts, to compel a full exposition and justification of all of them which anyone considers questionable, to censure them if found to merit condemnation . . ."
This function is the responsibility of members in all parts of the house. I do not condemn any party, but as a private member I say we are not discharging this function. Somebody will say to me that we have a public accounts committee. Reading Durell I find that there are three stages in finance -estimates, expenditures and accounting; and that there is a duty on the part of parliament to examine expenditures. I sometimes believe that if the government were to include in the estimates an item of $5 million for which there was no justification whatsoever, under our present system of examination in the House of Commons it could be passed. This is a serious matter. .
When one looks back over the years when government was less complex than it is today, when hon. members now on the other side of the house were on this side-
On both sides.

When the reverse
was the fact, there was an examination of expenditures.

A good opposition.
Interim Supply

I am not discussing the matter from that point of view. It is all very well to talk about a good opposition, but with the hundreds of millions of dollars expended today, and without members on the opposition side of the house having the necessary techniques and experts available to study the estimates, we in the House of Commons cannot discharge our responsibilities.
I rise solely for the purpose of suggesting that if we as members are to discharge our responsibility, the time has come to depart from parliamentary tradition, if you will, and make available to the opposition experts who will assist in the analysis of these accounts, without which an examination of the expenditures becomes a haphazard farce.
Somebody has said: What about the public accounts committee? There is no institution in Great Britain more effective than the public accounts committee. The reason is that it is a committee composed of members of the House of Commons-and I am quoting again from Durell:
. . . who have shown their interest in financial questions, even though, as opponents of the government, they might during the investigations of the committee obtain further facilities for criticizing its policy. It is recognized that the question of public accounts is a national and not a party question, and, as such, the investigation is made in the public interest and from a financial, not a political, point of view. Discussions in the house itself on financial questions, on the other hand, are apt to follow party lines, and the real issue is apt to be obscured.
I granted that the withholding or granting of supply is an important function of parliament, I suggest that something must be done in order to improve the techniques whereby members of the house can discharge their responsibility instead of pretending to discharge it when as a matter of fact they are unable to do so.
In the United Kingdom-and it may seem an unusual course to follow-the chairman of the public accounts committee is a member of the opposition, the purpose being to ensure a complete investigation of all expenditures made or asked for from parliament. My purpose in speaking at this time is to suggest that a committee be set up along the lines of the public accounts committee of the United Kingdom, which has done great work. That it is not actuated in any way by party considerations is indicated by the fact that the chairmanship is bestowed upon a member of the opposition.
If we are to discharge our responsibilities, we must be given information which today is unavailable to us. We ask these questions on the order paper day by day; we get some information, but not enough to give us an intelligent grasp of any one feature of these

Interim Supply
expenditures. For that reason I ask the government to give consideration to making available to those who are in opposition- and equally, of course, to members supporting the government-the services of experts, including the Auditor General, in order to make possible an intelligent examination of the accounts.
I did not rise to protest what was being done. What is in fact being done today is only a short-cut, the course that is followed in connection with all estimates. In one case we may talk about them in detail. On a motion such as this, of course, we do not discuss individual expenditures, but in any case there is not that examination which, with over-all expenditures of $2,500 million, the people of Canada have a right to expect on the part of members in all parts of the house.

I do not rise either to oppose or to support the argument made by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I merely wish to point out that the public accounts and the estimates are two different things. The estimates before us represent moneys not yet appropriated or expended, so that a discussion of the estimates is quite different from a discussion of the public accounts.
I have been in this house a fairly long time, and if there is any one thing which in my opinion you cannot keep free from political bias it is the public accounts, when the public accounts committee meets. That is quite natural, because when the public accounts committee meets, the opposition of course is looking for scandal or wrongdoing, and the government will do everything in its power to see that they do not find what they are looking for. There will be objections to giving information, and all that sort of thing. I believe we could have a committee on public accounts that would properly analyse these accounts if we set about it in the right way.
I believe there is a great deal to be desired in the way the estimates are dealt with in this house. We give too much time to a few departments, and hardly any time at all to a great many others. Every year as long as I have been here we have spent afternoon after afternoon and evening after evening on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. We have minutely examined every cutworm and every boll weevil in the prairie provinces, and we have investigated thoroughly the various functions of that department. But when we come to the estimates of other important departments, they go through this house at the rate of about a million dollars a minute, with no consideration whatever.

I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre to this extent at least, that we should attempt to devise some effective means of dealing with both the estimates and our public accounts.

Perhaps before the Minister of Finance replies I might briefly contribute two thoughts that have struck me.
The first has to do with the form of the estimates, to which attention has been drawn in previous years. That form is not such as to lend itself to a thorough analysis of our expenditures. Two years ago the Auditor General submitted to the public accounts committee detailed recommendations with respect to the form of the estimates and other matters, which he said would enable hon. members to conduct a detailed review and to fulfil their duty of satisfying themselves and the public that the expenditures sought by the government were proper. In the intervening two and a half years no action has been taken with respect to those useful and comprehensive recommendations coming from the Auditor General, and I would urge on the minister that the time has come when they should be given attention. They were the product of much thought and long experience on his part, and should receive consideration by the government.
My other thought has to do with an alternative procedure which has been tried by this house on previous occasions; and I mention this particularly in the hope of interesting the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The one exception to the ordinary rule that estimates are considered only in committee of supply, so far as I am aware, has been with respect to the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, since a standing committee on external affairs was first set up in 1945. In each of the intervening sessions the estimates of that department have been referred to the standing committee, and I am prepared to say that they have been given more careful review and more thorough analysis there than the estimates of any other department have received in committee of the whole house. The simple reason is that in the committee it has been possible to question officials of the department. The under-secretary has been there, and members of the committee have been afforded an opportunity of eliciting firsthand information which has been of the greatest value to them.
It is utterly impossible to carry on a detailed review and analysis of proposed expenditures, running into billions of dollars, under the clumsy, awkward procedure the house follows in committee of supply. As

every hon. member well knows, it is impossible to examine properly these heavy proposed expenditures in a committee which includes all members of the house, where there is no opportunity to direct questions to officials; where it is possible only to ask questions of the minister and to obtain from him information that he in turn has obtained from the officials sitting before him.
I am reminded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that on at least some occasions the accounts of Canadian National Railways have been reviewed by the sessional committee on government-owned railways.
There, it seems to me, we have two useful precedents which justify wider application of the method there pursued; and I do urge that consideration be given to extending this practice, and in particular that the minister be good enough to study the extensive recommendations made by the Auditor General to the public accounts committee in 1947.

I am sure the members of the government will appreciate the suggestions that have been offered by the hon. members who have just spoken.
The estimates are divided into two parts. In the first part the various items are listed, and in the second part there is a detailed statement of expenditures. In order to understand the whole thing, one must read the reports of the various departments which throw light on the items appearing in the estimates.
As to the public accounts, I shall give some comfort to the minister by reminding him that some years ago, on my protest, in which I was supported by the member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and the former member for Davenport, Mr. MacNicol, I succeeded in having the public accounts reformed. No member of the opposition had complained before about the fact that during the war no item less than $25,000 was mentioned in the estimates. It was only after the three of us complained to the then minister of finance- Mr. MacNicol called it an outrage-that we succeeded in obtaining this reform of the public accounts. The government should be given credit for that.
If the opposition wish to scrutinize the public accounts, they could divide themselves into various groups-in fact I believe that has been done. These groups could specialize in various departments and become familiar with certain aspects of public business. They could ask pertinent questions of the government. Questions on picayune matters should not be asked, and the members should abstain from theorizing during discussion of the estimates. The purpose of the committee of
Interim Supply
supply is to allow members to obtain supplementary information about the estimates that are before the committee. If we are to have never-ending speeches and repetition of the same thing by the same people every time an item is called, then there will be no end to the discussion.
The reason the discussion of estimates takes so much time is that so many members have no sense of proportion as to what is important and what is not. They waste much time on small detailed matters. If the members would consider the whole aspect of the matter in the first place, and then get down to particulars by asking questions so that they would be informed instead of trying to inform the government, more rapid progress would be made, and the procedure in passing the estimates would be more satisfactory to the members of the committee and to the public at large.

The member for Temiscouata has provided one of the best arguments I have heard for a change in our system of studying the public accounts. What the member for Eglinton said a few moments ago was only too true-that the two committees which have been examining the estimates of the railways and of the Department of External Affairs have worked to the benefit of both departments and of members of the house. I am in some agreement with the suggestion of the member for Temiscouata that if estimates are discussed in a committee there is a disposition to deal with them in a more businesslike manner. This is not so in the committee of supply.
Many of these items in the estimates are details that call for the immediate attention and presence of the officers of the department concerned. I do not think it is quite good enough to follow the old system, which has been followed for so many years, of proceeding in leisurely fashion in committee of supply with an examination of perhaps one department, and then, at the last moment, having a tremendous rush to complete the business before the house. No one is given a fair opportunity of dealing with the items in question. In at least some of our departments I believe we could well adopt the system suggested by the member for Eglinton, that is, the method which has worked so well in the external affairs and railways and shipping committees.
If the matter is dealt with in a standing or special committee, there is an opportunity for questioning of the departmental heads. In the committee of supply all one gets is an echo from the departmental heads through the ministry. The departmental head whispers something to the minister, and the

Interim Supply
minister pipes it back to the house. It would be much better if we were able to direct questions to the departmental officers. From my experience, the echo system of cross-examination does not work out very well, There are two other reasons why this change should be made, to enable us to examine the departmental heads from time to time. One has to do with the amount of time that the house ordinarily sits each year. I believe the length of the session could be cut down, without affecting the quality of the work done, if the major part of the estimates were brought before appropriate committees. Perhaps it would be proper to have the administration item for each department considered in the committee of supply, but the other items should go before the appropriate committee. If we did this I believe it would shorten our sessions and increase the efficiency of parliament.
Moreover, with about ninety new members of the house, and with a large proportion of the membership supporting the government, I can readily understand that there must be many members who are anxious to have more to do. It is difficult for a party with a hundred and ninety members to provide subject matter for discussion for the ordinary member. Every member, no matter in what part of the house he sits, has a responsibility to discharge to his constituents. They have sent him here for a specific purpose, namely, to do his part, along with the other members, in providing good government for Canada. Under a system such as I have suggested, I believe these members would find a way in which they could use their respective talents. It would make members feel they were part and parcel of the parliament of Canada, and not simply listening members for ninety-nine per cent of the time that parliament is in session. I wish to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he has given consideration to calling a meeting of external affairs committee for the purpose of considering the estimates of that department. His answer may be that he is not the officer responsible for calling the committee, but if the government intends to call the committee this year it ought to be done fairly soon, because it may be only a matter of weeks before the session concludes. I believe the committee ought to have a reasonable time to deal with the matters which will come before it.

This is the second interim supply biU we have been asked for, and it simply means that we are only holding a post mortem on these expenditures. In answer to the hon. member for Peterborough West, the minister expressed the hope that all of the estimates would be passed by the end of October. Next Monday is the end of October, and here the government are asking for another bill. The businessmen of the country expected some reduction. After all, it is important to the country. We can find no reduction in the expenditures. The Auditor General has been forgotten.
I want to thank the hon. member for Temiscouata for his remarks about the former member for Davenport, Mr. MacNicol, and myself. Years ago we did support here a new system in respect to interim supply and the public accounts. The principle of the bill before the committee is simply this. It means taxation without representation, the very principle upon which the thirteen original American colonies seceded, after the Boston tea incident. I do say that the public accounts committee should have been called to inquire into these expenditures. We are only holding a coroner's inquest into them. This is the second interim supply bill this session. I say that we should have some system whereby the Auditor General, the House of Commons and the public accounts committee should exercise some control over aU these expenditures. They are the forgotten people, so far as the government of Canada is concerned.

In this committee this afternoon we have listened to a discussion similar to others we have heard over a period of years. I would remind the committee that in 1945 or 1946 there was general agreement that some attempt should be made to refer as an experiment some of the estimates to appropriate committees in order that they might be looked into by those committees and reported to the house. The government agreed to that procedure, and so did the party which I have the honour to lead; but my recollection is that it was not agreed to by the official opposition at that time. I am glad we have had this afternoon this suggestion made by several members of the official opposition, because I feel that this is the way these estimates might be dealt with more effectively. Perhaps we can get general agreement in this chamber to try the experiment of having the estimates of some departments dealt with in this way.
While I am on my feet, may I say that the hon. member for Lake Centre this afternoon stated that we could elicit information from the government by way of questions. But may I point out that we do not always get

information from the government by way of questions. Indeed, the answers to questions sometimes exemplify the old proverb that some people can use words to conceal their thoughts. I know that some time ago I asked a question and it was answered on October 12. The question was:
1.	Did the government of Canada at any time from July 1. 1944, to July 30, 1949, make any offer to the government of Saskatchewan to help finance the trans-Canada highway on a fifty-fifty basis?
The Minister of Agriculture, from one end of that province to the other during the recent election campaign, said this had been done.
2.	If so, when was the offer made, and1 by whom?
The answer given by the minister of reconstruction was as follows:
1.	Possible bases of financial participation were indicated publicly and discussed between ministers of the federal government and the government of Saskatchewan.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
Yesterday I obtained a return of all the correspondence that had taken place on this particular matter between the federal government and the provincial government. In that correspondence I can find nothing that would warrant any statement of the type which was made by the Minister of Agriculture and which I was trying to verify. So when we are told that we can elicit information from the government by way of questions, I would point out that it has been demonstrated over and over again that we do not always get the information we ask for. I think the idea put forward by the hon. member for Lake Centre, the hon. member for Eglinton, the hon. member for Peel and others is something that the house and the various groups in the house should consider and try.
I support what the hon. member for Lake Centre has said with regard to the need of assistance to the opposition groups in the way of research and so on. In these days when we have so many activities and so many complex problems to deal with, it is impossible for individual members to dig up the information that is required. The advantage that the government has in dealing with these matters is perfectly obvious. There are the ministers, the ministerial assistants, the deputies and all the departmental officials. When a question comes up for discussion in the house, or when something is likely to be dealt with in the house, the ministers have all the assistance they require to get the information together for their own purposes. That is true not only in connection with the business of the house; I think many of us have reason to know that it is also true when public matters are being discussed in the country, whether it is during an election period or
Interim Supply
between elections, that the government side of the house has had an advantage all the time with regard to information. I hope that some way can be worked out to deal with the matter. The hon. member for Lake Centre suggested a way when he spoke of what was done in the British house with respect to the discussion of estimates; that procedure is rather different from the methods that we have been discussing this afternoon, but it indicates the attempt that has been made in what we sometimes call the mother of parliaments, to see to it that the public expenditures have a thorough investigation. Out of this discussion this afternoon I hope that something constructive will result.
May I just point out to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that I think he must be labouring under a misapprehension-
No, I am not.

-on the question of the committee being set up on estimates. I think it was in the year 1942 or 1943 that I made my first speech in the house advocating that particular procedure. I remember only one member of the house, and he did not happen to be on our side, who objected to the procedure which I suggested. I have repeated that suggestion and have taken substantially the same position today. I never heard anyone in our group who opposed me on the position I took. Perhaps the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is mistaken, because on many occasions we have asked for this procedure, and I have not heard of any division on it.

On that point, may I point out that the opposition agreed to the abstract principle when it was raised, but when the matter was put in concrete form and the committee was offered, they refused to accept it.
That is not true.
That is quite right.
When was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to this discussion, and I want to thank all those who have contributed to it for the objective way in which they have been considering the problem of an examination of the proposed public expenditures. I am not at all times in agreement with all the views expressed by my friend the hon. member for Lake Centre; but with a good many of those he has expressed today I am in agreement. I must say I do not think the House of Commons satisfactorily discharges its responsibility of examining in detail the estimates of proposed expenditures

Interim Supply
for a year. I have been here for eight or nine years now, and for seven or eight of those years I have been closely connected with the Department of Finance. As hon. members know, the estimates for the year in considerable detail are tabled in the house early in the session. If parliament commences in January, they are usually tabled by the middle of February. They set out the proposed expenditures of the government for the year. Departments are opened as rapidly as possible, but for understandable reasons there is considerable delay in getting all departments entered so that they can be discussed. Moreover, when we do come to consider the estimates themselves, my experience has been that the discussion rarely relates to the particular item of expenditure under consideration. It usually relates to agriculture in general, or to transport in general, or to something else; but it does not relate to the particular thousand-dollar item or million-dollar item which may be before the committee.
If I may say so, in my experience in the House of Commons, with only one or two rare exceptions, I have heard no suggestion made to reduce any item under consideration. That, again, is understandable. I made a statement once in the house that the only place where reductions in expenditures were made was in my office. I said that, because that is the place where treasury board meets, and where we consider the expenditures of the various departments.
I do believe that the practice of consideration of departmental estimates can be better organized than it is at the present time. My hon. friend from Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) quite properly pointed out that the function of the committee of supply of the house, to examine proposed expenditures, is quite different from that of the public accounts committee, whose function it is to consider expenditures long after they have been made, in order to see whether or not they were properly made-and if they were not properly made to make a recommendation as to how the practice should be changed in the future.
Then, as to the suggestion that expert assistance should be made available to afford members of parliament in general, and perhaps members in opposition groups in particular, an opportunity to know what the real details of estimates are, let me say, as I said before, that the individual items and the details in the book of estimates itself are available early in the session.
I cannot speak for departments other than my own, but with respect to my own department I can say-and I feel it applies to other departments as well-that any member of

parliament who asks either the minister or the permanent head of a department for information as to the details of a particular item in the estimates will receive that information.
I receive such requests fairly frequently from members-not as often as one might expect-but I do receive them, and endeavour to see that the information asked for is furnished.
So, if I may venture to offer the suggestion,
I believe the remedy in great part lies with ourselves; and if we do not take up too much time debating matters other than those relating to public expenditures, and if when we do consider the estimates and restrict our discussion to the particular item before the committee, then perhaps the proposed expenditures will receive more detailed consideration than they do at the present time.
Just one final word as to the suggestion that we change the system, and that we have the estimates considered by special committees of the house. That procedure has been applied in only one case, namely in respect of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. They have been referred to a special committee.
And those of the Canadian National Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That committee considers the budget of the Canadian National Railways, not the estimates. The committee on railways owned and operated by the government is each year furnished with the capital budget of the railways and, I believe, with the operating statement. But those are not estimates; they are the regular railway budget. They are not departmental estimates voted by parliament.
The only items upon which the house is bound to vote, and which are considered in special committee, are the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. I am not a member of that committee, but I am told it has proved to be a most satisfactory committee. Perhaps it has been particularly satisfactory because foreign affairs in this parliament, as in the parliament at Westminster, have been dealt with almost entirely on a strictly nonpartisan basis. There is never any question of partisanship entering into a discussion of external affairs. I have been told that in considering the estimates in that committee, as has been the case in the house, not too much attention is paid to the particular item in the estimates under consideration. Perhaps under the estimate for an embassy in some European capital the discussion is likely to range over Canada's policy with respect to the United Nations, or something else of that kind. However, as I say, I am speaking only

from hearsay. I am personally not satisfied that the committees system can be used generally under our British parliamentary system.
The point has been made that permanent officials should be made available before these committees to be examined as to details of expenditures. In a special case I think that is all right; but we must not lose sight of the fact that under our system the responsible minister must come to parliament, state his policy, state his items of expenditure and take the responsibility for them.
The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) has suggested that the minister is only the echo of the deputy minister, who gives the minister the information. I think that is not a fair statement, nor is it accurate. When we are in committee of the whole considering the estimates of a department, the minister of that department will have his officials in front of him. Then, when a question comes up, we will say, in connection with the experimental farm at Lethbridge, the amount to be spent and what it will be used for, the minister may consult his deputy minister, or whoever the official may be. But the minister gives the information to the house and takes the responsibility for it.
I must confess that I believe if we were to engage in any widespread system of committees examining expenditures, and of submitting permanent civil servants to long attendance before those committees to furnish details of departmental estimates, we would find that the public service might be seriously interfered with, aside altogether from the propriety under our system of questioning permanent officials on matters of policy.
Another reason I have always felt it is not desirable to delegate to committees the responsibility which rests with the House of Commons in connection with the detailed consideration of expenditures is that every single member of the house is entitled to look at the expenditures and to ask questions with respect to them. That is the traditional right of any member of parliament. I do not think we can delegate that right to any committee.
I am not saying that for certain special types of expenditures or special public services it might not be desirable, as obtains in connection with the estimates for the Department of External Affairs, to have the estimates in such cases referred to appropriate committees for consideration. However, I do not think that that can be accepted as a substitute for the general consideration which should be given in committee of the whole.
I was impressed by the suggestion made the other day by the hon. member for Peel that, in arranging for the introduction of 45781-74i

departments, such departments should be entered as promptly as possible, and that the items for administration of as many departments as possible should be called in fairly early rotation, so that a general discussion could take place with respect to several departments in the early stages of the session. Admittedly many of the items appearing in departmental estimates do not call for extensive consideration. But if, instead of taking up eight or ten days in committee of supply to consider the estimates of one department, we were to alternate with others, I think it would be a better system. For that reason I would thoroughly agree with the views expressed the other night and repeated today.
I believe this has been a most helpful discussion. Hon. members who have presented their views have done so in a wholly objective manner. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has stated frankly that he does not place the blame on any party or group, and that this was a matter concerning which the responsibility rested with parliament. That is a view which I share completely, and I believe if we will all co-operate we can improve upon our present system of considering estimates and expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand it is the intention again this year to refer the estimates of the Department of External Affairs to the committee on external affairs.

I am glad to hear the Minister of Finance say that it is intended to refer the estimates of the Department of External Affairs to the standing committee on external affairs for review.
I should like to make one or two brief comments on the observations of the minister with regard to the conduct of affairs in the committee on external affairs and in committee of supply. The minister said that it was not proper for members of the house to delegate their responsibility, and I take it that he meant to a committee. There has never been any suggestion that any member of the House of Commons was delegating his responsibility to that committee when the estimates of that department were referred to it. The estimates were referred to the committee after there had been some opening discussion in the house and what the committee did was to sift the items. I wish to say to the minister that I do not think the information to which he referred as hearsay is accurate. Certainly it is not complete because in that committee-I speak from personal experience because I have been a member of it since its beginning-there has been a detailed review of every item. Information was asked for by members of the committee and supplied by the departmental officials. Breakdowns of the items were supplied and we were given information as to expenditures in previous years. With ^ the figures right in front of us we were in a position to compare the proposed expendi-
ture with the actual expenditure in the previous year. As I say, the committee carried on the task of sifting. When the items came back to the house there was no restriction on the right of any member to obtain whatever information he thought he should obtain. But considerable information had been obtained already and considerable time of the house was saved by the work done in that committee.
In this connection I should like to call attention to a specific recommendation made to the house in 1947 by the public accounts committee. I have already mentioned the fact that the Auditor General made lengthy and detailed recommendations on this subject with the view of ensuring that the House of Commons would carry out its traditional responsibility to review proposed expenditures before voting supply. The Minister of Finance has drawn attention to the distinctive functions of the public accounts committee. It does review expenditures, but unfortunately that review cannot be made until at least a year and a half after the expenditures have been made. The work of reviewing estimates is an entirely different matter. It was with that in mind and after hearing the Auditor General that the public accounts committee made a recommendation to be found at page 551 of the proceedings of the committee for 1947. This recommendation reads as follows:
Your committee is also of the opinion that the government should explore the desirability of establishing a standing committee on estimates.
Let us be frank about this matter. If one committee is charged with the responsibility of reviewing the estimates of all departments it will have a heavy task to perform. There are limits to the time that an hon. member can devote to a committee, but it seems to me that that recommendation at least points to the direction in which the house must proceed in modernizing its procedure if a really serious attempt is to be made to discharge our responsibilities as members of the House of Commons in the voting of public money.
Much could be done, and the Auditor General has pointed this out, to improve the form in which estimates are presented to the house. At the present time the information given in the volume of estimates is of only two kinds. There is the proposed expenditure or estimate for the current year which the government asks the house to vote, and then in the second column is shown the amount which was voted by parliament in the previous year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And the details at the back of the book.

I am referring to the nature of the information. The details given in the later pages are of the item to be voted but nowhere in the volume is there information as to the actual expenditure in the preceding year. Surely that is the sort of guide that hon. members need to assist them in deciding how much should be voted for a particular item for the current year. It should not be too difficult to get that information. The Auditor General recommended that that information should be given in the printed volume of estimates. He pointed out that it would save much time by eliminating the asking of questions about actual expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In my experience it has seldom been possible at the time the estimates are printed to have available the actual expenditures in the preceding year. My hon. friend will appreciate that the estimates for the fiscal year are usually prepared in November or December. As a matter of fact I am writing to the departments today asking them to have their departmental estimates in for consideration by the treasury board by the end of November. However, they are seldom finalized, if I may use that word, until the middle of January. It is not always possible to have available at that time the actual expenditures in the previous year, but that information is almost invariably available when the item comes up for consideration in committee.

I had that point in mind and I was just going to speak about it. The suggestion was made that as the printed volume was prepared toward the end of the fiscal year it would be possible at that time to give actual expenditures for eight or nine months of the fiscal year, with an estimate of anticipated expenditure for the balance of the year. That was also discussed in the public accounts committee.
Then with regard to obtaining information in the committee of supply, I have had some experience with the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare for several years. In an earnest attempt to save the time of the committee I asked the minister -this is a matter of record, at least for 1947 and 1948 and for other years as well-when the first item was under consideration to supply the committee with a breakdown of expenditures in the preceding year. With that information it would not have been necessary to ask questions on each individual item. However, each time I have been met with a firm refusal by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and I was forced to take up time on each item to ask for the corresponding expenditure in the preceding fiscal year. I say that was a ridiculous waste of
Interim Supply
time. There is no reason at all why a minister, coming before the committee of supply with his estimates, should not be in a position at the very outset to supply the committee with a complete statement of the actual expenditures of the previous fiscal year item by item. That will save the committee of supply much time.
I should like to refer to two of the recommendations of the Auditor General to be found at page 429 of the proceedings of the public accounts committee of 1947. The second recommendation is in these words:
There may have been a time when the committee of supply minutely examined estimate items, but demands now made on the time of the House of Commons are such that complete examination of estimates is impracticable. Estimates should now be presented in such a form that members do not have to guess purposes to which votes will be applied.
In his third recommendation he says:
It is suggested that, instead of members of parliament having to seek explanations from ministers, "details" printed with the estimates should be in narrative form, setting out (a) the objects and purposes of the items; (b) explanations of increases; (c) the acts, if any, which will regulate application; (d) the anticipated revenues; (e) comparisons with previous years, and (f) such other information as is necessary to permit members to familiarize themselves with the purposes and implications before items are called by the chairman of the committee of supply.
These recommendations were the product of the thought and long experience of the Auditor General, one of the most respected officials in the entire public service of Canada.
I have one final comment to make on the minister's suggestion-and I cannot refrain from calling it a bogey-that we are challenging the principle of ministerial responsibility whenever we propose that a committee of the house should be established. Surely when the committee is simply appointed by the house, has to report back to the house, and the house takes the responsibility for everything that is done, it cannot fairly be said that there is any breach of the principle of responsibility.
In this parliament above all previous parliaments it seems to me more necessary than ever that members should be afforded every opportunity to obtain information, and to see that the house, with its large government majority, functions efficiently, and that the fullest possible information is made available in order that the house may study the problems before it.
I think that will apply particularly to the voting of supply. There are nearly one hundred new members in the house, every one of whom, along with those who have been

Interim Supply
here before, will profit by additional information and in other ways from the opportunities afforded in a committee of eliciting useful information, which are not afforded in the big committee of supply with a procedure that is so clumsy, in relation to a task of this kind, as to make it impossible for us to discharge our duties properly.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the discussion this afternoon has been one of the must useful that has taken place since the beginning of the session. In replying to the remarks that have been made, the Minister of Finance said that a large part of the remedy lies with the members. The whole debate has taken place on a basis that is in keeping with the importance of the subject that has been brought forward. I think we can go further, however, and say that the whole remedy lies with members of the house because this is the only place, subject to the concurrence or otherwise of another place, in which the remedy for the situation can be found.
I do not think that the discussion should be allowed to end where it is now. Many constructive suggestions have been made, and the fact that they are constructive has been shown by the response of the Minister of Finance to what has been said. There are some points which perhaps have not been sufficiently emphasized in relation to what has taken place in the last few years. The system under which the house is called upon to exercise its greatest responsibility, that of providing supply, is one that was devised for a time when expenditures authorized by the house were smaller than those of some of the individual provinces today in their own fields.
At a time when expenditures placed before the house were only a small fraction of what they are now, it may well have been possible to examine each item and to consider it in that measure of detail that is consistent with the need for actual knowledge of what the item means before it is passed, if that approval is to mean anything. The minister has said that when items come up for discussion a great deal of time may be spent upon one department, and in the case of another department spending as much or more hardly any time at all may be devoted to a number of items. There is a simple explanation for that fact. In the case of agriculture and other departments where a number of members have a ready knowledge of the type of things for which the money is appropriated, it is much easier for them to ask questions which are related to the real purpose for which the money is set aside. But with the increasingly

complex requirements of government administration, and with the many completely new fields into which government has entered in the past few years, there are many items about which most members have little information from their own past experience. Consequently, without an extended crossexamination of the minister as to the details that lie behind even a very large item, it may not be possible to secure a clear picture of the purpose for which that amount is included in the estimates.
I think there is a misconception in the suggestion frequently made in the house that it is not in keeping with our parliamentary system that there should be a delegation of ministerial responsibility to committees. There is no suggestion of delegation of ministerial responsibility if a subject under consideration by the house is placed before a committee so that members of the house may have all the information they should have before they are called upon to ask the minister those questions which will bring out all the facts that the house should have before reaching a decision. On the contrary, our system implies full knowledge of all essential details in the possession of every member, whether or not he is a supporter of the government. That is the very foundation of our parliamentary system. No matter how intricate the subject may be, no matter how long it may take to obtain the essential information, our system can only function if every member of the house is able to obtain information which enables him to reach a decision with full knowledge of every relevant fact.
Now that this discussion has arisen this problem should be met and a solution found. Our whole system has advanced through examination of the procedure and developments related to the expanding responsibilities of the government and the parliament which is called upon to approve the actions of that government. There is a great difference between the public accounts committee and the examination of the estimates, which was emphasized in the first instance by the hon. member for Lake Centre when he dealt with this subject. The reports of the Auditor General themselves constitute the strongest possible argument for an improvement in our system of dealing with estimates. Year after year the Auditor General refers to some item where the procedure should have been different; and in a number of instances large and important items are referred to in a way that indicates quite clearly that hon. members were not aware of what really were the details concerning those matters. If this subject is to be dealt with effectively we must approach

it on the basis of the scale of governmental responsibility today, and seek to find a solution that will make it possible for hon. members to fulfil their responsibilities and also to avoid unnecessary debate, which could be eliminated if the necessary facts could be obtained in another way. One of the most important problems facing this parliament is to find a way of shortening its sessions, without in any way limiting opportunities for debate. It will become increasingly difficult for men and women across Canada to offer themselves as candidates for parliament if the sittings of this house continue to increase in length year by year. The effective use of committees of the house is one way in which the session could be shortened*, at the same time permitting parliament to discharge its duties more efficiently. If these estimates were referred to the committees whose activities relate to their subject matter, there would be no delegation of ministerial responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said a delegation of parliamentary responsibility, not ministerial responsibility.
There was a time when we mentioned ministerial responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not mean to suggest that it was a delegation of ministerial responsibility.

Then let me say there would be no delegation of parliamentary responsibility, because the very existence of the committees indicates quite clearly that their activities have never been regarded as a delegation of parliamentary responsibility. This whole system of committees is embedded in our parliamentary system, and has been for many years; and the purpose for which committees have been provided is to give hon. members an opportunity to obtain information that will facilitate and expedite the business of the house. If a committee dealt with the estimates of a particular department and the experts and departmental officials were brought before that committee, with plenty of time at their disposal the members of the committee, representing both sides of the house, could obtain essential information in a way that is not possible here in the house, where a member may only ask questions of the minister. Then the minister quite frankly finds it necessary to lean over and ask his departmental officials for the answer. He is given that answer either orally or on a slip of paper, and that limited information is what comes back to the member.
Let us not pretend that this system is nearly as satisfactory as one under which members from both sides of the house could
Interim Supply
ask appropriate officials exactly what is involved. I want to emphasize that I do not think anyone on this side has been suggesting that such questioning should relate to whether the officials think the department could be better operated or better run, but certainly those who are called upon to discuss these questions have the same right as the government itself to know whether there might be an alternative method of presenting these figures, whether they could be presented in simpler form, or whether they could be placed before the house in a way that would provide more information. That is the sort of questions that might be asked. When that information was obtained the various details could be secured which would make it possible for those members in turn to be fully prepared to come into the house and deal with the estimates in a way that would save time here.
As was pointed out, the estimates of the Department of Agriculture take a very long time. Probably they would take a very short time if the committee had the opportunity of examining them in advance. Hon. members belonging to that committee could obtain the information they require, and then would be able to present their opinions as to what should be done and, of course, in the general discussion of the estimates they would offer suggestions as to how the administration of the department could be improved or changed.
We must remember that the public accounts committee can only deal with accounts which are practically two years old. What is essential here is that hon. members be placed in a position where, with equal efficiency, they can deal with the items they are required to pass upon, concerning future expenditure. As has been pointed out on a number of occasions, there is a great difference between our system and that of the United States. However, we can perhaps consider what happens there, because they are handling enormous sums of money. All their estimates do go before committees, where they are subject to the most searching examination.

Under our system, the minister takes the responsibility of presenting the figures that have been prepared by his officials. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the United States, there is not responsible government; that is the fundamental difference.

I recognize that difference, but in the end we come back to the responsibility of the minister. We must remember that, as the minister himself has pointed out, we are talking about the responsibility of parliament as well. We have not only a system of responsible government, but we have a system of responsible parliament and that also is different from the United States system. Under our system of a responsible parliament, just as under our system of responsible government, there is that essential difference. In the end, however, we must assume the responsibility; in one case, the minister for presenting the figures, and in the other case, the members for passing them.
Under our system of responsible government, the minister has the opportunity of asking each official any detail that he wants. Every member of this house, Mr. Chairman, has a duty to have every essential fact before he passes upon the figures that have been presented by the minister. With the tremendous expenditures that are now put before us, there is no way in which this house will be able to deal effectively with this subject, unless some procedure is devised by which essential information may be obtainable which is not made available in this house. I repeat that we have not an opportunity of examining the experts. The experts are here to advise the minister, as quickly as possible and as comprehensibly as possible, in regard to questions that are asked on the floor of the house. That procedure does not elicit the information which each of us should be able to get.
Now, as an alternative method of obtaining information from departmental officials, which was partly implied by the minister, I feel sure that legitimate objection would be raised if a constant unorganized effort were made to obtain this kind of information. It would create confusion. I am not suggesting for one moment that there is any desire to prevent the members obtaining the information. One could easily imagine, however, the confusion that would result if, according to their own whim, any one of the members at any time attempted to detach officials from a department for the purpose of conducting

his own inquiry into those accounts. It could create confusion which might impair the efficiency of any department.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the discussion that has taken place this afternoon indicates that now is the time to tackle this problem. The minister admits that we have passed the time when the older system fully meets our requirements. Many of the members have made it quite clear that they do not believe they can obtain the information they should have in this way. Above all, there is a necessity for using another system to shorten the inquiry which takes place in this house, and which in many cases is lengthened simply because of the system we now have.
While it is not possible to put this forward in the form of a motion, in view of the statement made by the minister that the answer rests with ourselves, I do urge that he give immediate consideration to the advisability of setting up a small select committee of this house to consider and recommend an improved procedure for examining and dealing with estimates of expenditures placed before this house. If that is done, then the work of the minister as well as the work of the members will be facilitated and we shall have started back towards a responsible parliamentary system. It is all very well for us to talk about a responsible parliamentary system, but the test of our responsibility is the extent to which we pass supply with knowledge of those facts that assure that we have accepted our responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I just want to make one comment in connection with my hon. friend's remarks. I know that the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) wants to say something. In part, what I had in mind when I said the remedy lies with ourselves was that, before we go too far in changing our system, I would appeal to the hon. members to make use of what already exists. In this book of estimates which I hold in my hand, there are over two hundred pages in fine print. Those pages contain details, rather specific and comprehensive details, of the various services. Before I was a parliamentary assistant and before I was a minister, I was a private member. I am free to confess that even for those departments in which I was interested, I never took the time or trouble to examine any of the details of an item until that item came up in the house. Perhaps I was an exception, but I do not think so.
I believe it is fair to say that the majority of members, through pre-occupation with other important matters, do not spend a great deal of time studying this volume which is tabled every year about February 15. I agree with my hon. friend that if every member of

parliament went haphazardly to the heads of the different departments and requested specific information about every item, it would mean a very heavy burden on the department. If any member of parliament, however, takes any single item in this book of estimates and, after examining the detail in the back of the book, desires further detailed information about that item, I can assure him that the departmental officials will give him every bit of information that they give to the minister of the department concerned. That does not mean, of course, that there will be time available in the house for the careful, detailed consideration that perhaps some members would want to give. I simply say this: do not let us condemn the system or the lack of information until we organize our own debates so as to facilitate the discussion and as long as we fail to make use of the information which is available.

I see the Minister of Labour has just come in, and I wish to take one item in his department to illustrate something that I have said a number of times in this house. The estimates do not give the full details for any department. Even if you look in the section for the department concerned, you cannot find all the expenditures of that department.
Although the Minister of Labour is responsible for unemployment insurance, we have to go to the public works department to find added figures with regard to the unemployment insurance commission. It is quite a chore to go through all these items to find the details for one item. There is page after page for buildings that are rented by the Department of Public Works in the province of Ontario, which are put at the disposal of the Minister of Labour. The Department of Public Works pays for the construction of those buildings in some cases, the improvements, repairs, rents, salaries of cleaners, furnace men, the coal, water, light and elevators; everything in connection with the building. Those amounts, however, are not chalked up against the Department of Labour. If our estimates and our accounts were run in the way a business company would run them, we would not have estimates in this style. We would have estimates that would be easy to read and that any businessman could check easily on the minister's items alone instead of having to go to other sections.
I notice under unemployment insurance you go all down the line, Fort William, Galt, Gananoque, Gloucester township and so on, page after page. After checking for other items, in Ontario alone there is almost $600,000 extra that we have to check into in 45781-75

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will answer my hon. friend in this way. It has purchased buildings, maintained them and repaired them for other departments. That has been one of the traditional functions of the Department of Public Works. I think that in some cases-and my colleague the Minister of Public Works will correct me if I am wrong-there is included in the departmental estimates an item to reimburse the Department of Public Works for expenditures which are made on behalf of that department. I could not find it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Possibly we should make some changes in that system. That is the sort of thing I should be glad to consider. I have listened with interest to the opinions expressed here, and I should be glad to discuss with the comptroller of the treasury and the departmental officials whether the method of set-up of the accounts can be changed to make them more clearly understandable. In fairness to my own department and to my own officials, I want to say that I am convinced that the public accounts today are presented in a clear and comprehensive fashion. In my personal experience I have had a good deal to do with seeing to the presentation of accounts; and as public accounts go, I think the public accounts of Canada are clearly presented and clearly understandable. That does not mean that they are perfect. It does not mean that there cannot be made changes which would make them clearer still. In answer to my hon. friend with respect to public works items, I can simply tell him, what he well knows, that that has been the method, probably since confederation, of presenting these figures.

I understand that. But during the first years of confederation little money was spent. It was a matter of only a few million dollars. Now the figures are up into the billions, and I really believe that a change should be made. I mention the fact that the Department of Public Works takes care of a number of other departments but at the same time the treasury officers of the Department of Public Works are paid for by the Department of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That applies to other departments.

That applies to the other departments; but because of the fact that it applies to the other departments, it does not at the same time give a true picture of any department because a number of officials in each department are paid for by a different department. I feel that even those treasury officers should be charged up to the proper department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will answer my hon. friend in this way. He is dealing with an accounting matter, namely the provision of treasury officers in the Department of Public Works or in any other department. They are in effect performing the functions of internal auditors, and in an ordinary commercial corporation they would be charged up to the corporation.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But in this case the corporation is the Dominion of Canada.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In a private corporation the internal audit in the sales department or in the manufacturing department is not necessarily charged up to that department as such. It is probably charged up to general overhead because that is what in fact it is. I am not an expert accountant, although I have considerable knowledge of accountancy. As I say, there may be a clearer way of presenting these estimates, but I do not think it is misleading to have the treasury officers who perform the function in the Department of Public Works charged up to that department and the treasury officers in the other departments charged up to those departments. It all comes back to the same place in the end, that is, to the taxpayers of Canada generally. As long as the system is understood by those who are considering it, I do not think there can be a great deal of misunderstanding on that point.

Does the Minister of Finance not think that a greater use could be made of the public accounts committee? We have an Auditor General who is exceptionally capable, one of the senior officials of the government, who reports-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To parliament.

And he reports directly to parliament. Each year he brings down a very comprehensive report, in my opinion a report which is well worthy of study. Then nothing happens. I think once or twice that report has been referred to the public accounts committee; but the discussion in committee has been more or less at random, and certainly not undertaken in a thorough way.
It does seem to me that is one of the great weaknesses in our system of checking expenditures. I realize that in the past the public accounts committee has been used as a political committee. I remember different questions being referred to it-such as the Bren gun inquiry, in which I took part myself. Then, there have been conducted by that committee other inquiries which were political in their nature.
But it does seem to me there is work of a non-political nature which could be done by that committee, namely carefully reviewing the report of the Auditor General. There are 50 members on the public accounts committee, and if they were given the opportunity to review the public accounts they would acquire a pretty fair knowledge of the expenses incurred by the government. They would be able to make many sugges-

I want to answer the hon. member on that, because I think unintentionally he has not been quite fair. This matter of the public accounts committee is one place in which parliament, as distinct from the government, can exercise its responsibility.
As my hon. friend knows, the public accounts committee is a standing committee of the House of Commons, and it is open to any member to ask that the committee be called together. And so far as I am aware- and this is certainly true since I have been Minister of Finance-no government has refused, or been reluctant to move to have the public accounts for a particular year referred to that committee. I know that, without the slightest fear of successful contradiction. I assert now that this is the place where parliament, as distinct from the government, can exercise its responsibility.
The Auditor General is an officer of the House of Commons, and the public accounts committee is a standing committee of the house. It is open to my hon. friend or to any other member to ask that that committee be set up and organized, and that the public accounts be referred to it-and I personally would be very happy, and have always been very happy, to refer the public accounts to that committee.

It is not the responsibility of the government to initiate a reference to the committee on public accounts.

We will be able to deal with the accounts that are before us now during the next session. Having said that, and having supported what has been said by other members in regard to the desirability of a wider use of the public accounts committee, I emphasize that my proposal for the setting up of a select committee did not relate to the public accounts but to the examination of the estimates so that we might be really prepared to assume the greatest responsibility that we are called upon to assume as members.
When the Minister of Finance says that at the back of this book are a number of pages containing details, and suggests that perhaps we do not examine those details, I think hon. members will recall that when estimates were under examination before hon. members displayed a considerable knowledge of the details. It is the necessity of going behind those details that we are discussing. No one has suggested any impropriety in the form; what is being suggested is that there should be an easy and workable method by which essential information can be obtained.
Let us take one example, the Department of National Defence estimates for the equipment and supplies required by that department. Under broad reference in each department expenditures of some $218 million are provided for. No one can tell by examining those items what are the essential details, and yet these items equal the total expenditures by the government of Canada a comparatively few years ago. All that is suggested is that we find some mechanism by which hon. members can in an orderly way, and assuming their responsibilities for supply, find out what the details are so that when they come into the house the items can be discussed with full knowledge. It was in relation to that suggestion and only to that suggestion that I made the proposal for a select committee.

Possibly as a new member I should not get up on this occasion, but I have listened to the statements made this afternoon, some of which have indicated that hon. members think the sessions should be shortened. I say now that I will not go back to my constituency and say that I am in favour of more business of parliament being done in some of the little anterooms in this building. I contend that open discussions in this chamber are the very pillars of democracy. The very essence of our parliamentary system lies in the fact that we have the right to say: Mr. Speaker-or Mr. Chairman-we would like to know this or that, or we believe

this or that. With these four galleries around us, I maintain that this chamber is the place in which to transact most of the nation's business. I quite agree that possibly there should be adopted some method whereby we can become more rapidly familiar with the operations of the various departments, but I think each party can make a start by instituting study groups if they wish to acquaint new members with the workings of the different departments of government. It is suggested that the proposed plan will shorten the sessions of parliament, but let me say that at times the percentage of attendance has not been very high in some quarters of the house since the session began. Perhaps they want a still shorter session. I would not like to see the system changed so that more would be done in committees and less in the house.

Mr. Chairman, my colleagues and I are fully prepared to support the proposal that a committee be set up for the purpose of endeavouring to determine more effective methods of dealing with the estimates. We quite properly disagree, however, that we should guess, as it were, what the possible outcome might be of such action. It has been indicated this afternoon that all the estimates should be referred to committees of the house. Naturally we hold individual opinions as to the result of such an action. Personally I find it extremely difficult to agree that, by referring all the estimates to various committees, satisfactory results would be obtained. I think of the multitude of new committees that would have to be set up. I think of committees sitting concurrently and making it utterly impossible for an individual member to attend all of them, or even to attend when matters of special interest to him were being considered. I can conceive of such committees sitting morning, afternoon and night in order to accomplish their purpose.
Some emphasis has been laid on the necessity of shortening our sessions. I am not quite so certain that that should be our objective. In my opinion the objective should be greater efficiency, and not necessarily shorter sessions. Of course, if the two could be achieved in one move that would be fine, but those of us who have been here for a considerable period of time realize that we really move swiftly during the last month of any session of parliament. Will any hon. member say that our most effective work is done during that period or that the word "efficiency" would be a proper one to associate with our actions at that time?
With respect to the information that is available in connection with the estimates, I would be the first to admit that there is far more information available than I have made use of. Agriculture was referred to
