speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Lake Centre) moved:
subtopic: SUGGESTED ADVISABILITY OF INTRODUCING A DECLARATION OF RIGHTS
SUGGESTED ADVISABILITY OF INTRODUCING A DECLARATION OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
I think I should point out that this resolution may be out of order on the same grounds as the resolutions previously moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). The first portion of the resolution contains these words:
-immediate consideration should be given to the advisability of introducing a bill or declaration of rights-
This, of course, does not constitute an instruction to the government. However, I would ask hon. members to look at the last paragraph of the resolution. The words "immediate consideration should be given to the advisability of" do not apply to or govern the concluding portion of the motion, which requires unconditionally that as a preliminary step the Minister of Justice shall submit a question to the Supreme Court of Canada. This purports to convey a direct order to the government to do something which could not be done without an expenditure of public money. I would think the first part of the resolution would be in order, but in my opinion the latter part would be out of order; and if part of a resolution is out of order the whole resolution is out of order.
Unless anyone would like to offer any comments, I am prepared to rule now that the resolution is out of order.
Before calling the next resolution may I state that I regret finding it necessary to declare a resolution out of order merely on technical grounds. I have given the matters some consideration and have spoken to the chief of the orders and notices branch suggesting that, when a resolution is handed to him which appears to be out of order on the ground that it would involve the payment of public money, he should bring that point to the attention of the hon. member who has filed the resolution. The hon. member could then quite easily change a few words and the resolution would be in order. As a matter of fact I have almost come to the conclusion that in future, when a notice of motion is out of order on technical grounds, I will give the hon. member an opportunity to modify his resolution, provided he does not widen its scope. I believe that would be only fair. I do not believe resolutions coming under the heading of notices of motions should be ruled out of order on mere technical grounds.
(Mr. Diefenbaker.]

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE ON PROPORTION OF FRENCH CANADIAN APPOINTMENTS
PROPOSED COMMITTEE ON PROPORTION OF FRENCH CANADIAN APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
That, In the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the establishment of a special committee, during the present session, to examine the advisability of granting to the French Canadians the proportion and classes of civil service positions to which they are entitled.
(Translation):
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to draw the government's attention to the important problem of French Canadian representation in the federal civil service and to point out the necessity for essential reforms in the operation of the whole machinery of the commission.
Need I add that my intention is not to blame the present administration for conditions that existed before it assumed power? On the contrary, I am pleased to note that since Mr. Mackenzie King's successor took up his duties, the situation about which my fellow citizens rightly complain today has somewhat improved. On the other hand I submit, and my claims are based on indisputable facts which it would be too long to recall here, that French Canadians hold neither the number nor the class of federal civil service positions to which they are entitled by their population figures and do not receive fair treatment from the parties responsible for the allotment of positions.
We have had sufficient proof of this in the apparent interest of the previous administration in this matter. I might recall that a group of members from the right headed by the former Solicitor General, was assigned the task of investigating the causes of and of suggesting a remedy to this increasingly alarming situation.
No report was ever published on this investigation. I would ask the government today to appoint an official committee comprising members from all political groups in this house, in order to carry out a full investigation on the situation as regards the French Canadian people in the federal civil service and to submit conclusions to the house.
The best way to promote national unity is to grant minorities their just dues. My fellow-citizens ask for no favours, no privileges. They do not care for that. All we want is a tangible recognition of our rights. If we look into the past, we find that in 1918, civil servants numbered 54,169 of which 41,618 were permanent. Sessional paper No.

301,919, of 1918, gives an individual list of 16,184 permanent employees, of which 3,493 or 21-58 per cent were French-speaking. From this date onward, the representation of French-speaking Canadians in the federal civil service has unfortunately been reduced. Thus, the Auditor General's report for the year 1945 shows that French Canadians held only 12J per cent of all positions commanding a yearly salary of $2,400 or more.
As far as deputy ministerships are concerned, the percentage of French-speaking deputy ministers dropped from 14-28 in 1918 to naught in 1946.
Today, out of 19 deputy ministers, we have three, exactly half of what we are entitled to.
The 1941 census showed that the total population of Canada reached 11,506,855 and that the French-speaking population was 30-27 per cent of the whole.
However, in 1946, according to a table prepared by the Ottawa Journal under date of April 4 of that same year, out of 37 officials who were deputy ministers or held comparable rank, five only were French Canadians. The former received $313,500 annually, against $38,500 for the latter. Among these was the Dominion Archivist, Mr. Lanctot, replaced in 1948 by Mr. Lamb. This caused Mr. Eugene L'Heureux to write in Le Soleil, on September 16, 1948, that Canadians of good will found this appointment somewhat surprising, to say the least, and that the principle of alternation should have been respected by choosing Mr. Donald Fee as Archivist and Mr. Marion as his assistant.
Mr. L'Heureux continues:
That would have been fair and reasonable. After all the official bilingualism which must form the very basis of our confederation does not require that key positions be divided into French Canadian territories and English Canadian territories but, as far as possible, the alternation of French and English Canadians in all positions.
Otherwise it would be admitting that one group is qualified for certain functions but unqualified for others. We cannot admit that. In the first place it is contrary to facts and in the second place, it goes against our pride.
To let French Canadians predominate at the Archives, for instance, while they are excluded from the Department of Finance would be an utterly unacceptable solution of the public service problem. We want our share, and no more than our share of influence and salaries, in each of the federal departments whenever we are qualified on the score not only of ability but also of educational training and practical experience.

(Translation):
Because they do not have their rightful number of civil service positions, the French Canadians are each year losing millions of dollars, besides the influence they could exert in the federal administration in the best interests of the country. The Chambre de Commerce of Montreal submitted to the Gordon commission, appointed by order in council on February 15,	1946, a quite exhaustive brief dealing with the federal civil service and with the place which Frenchspeaking Canadians occupy therein. The businessmen and members of the professional classes in the Canadian metropolis deserve to be warmly congratulated and thanked for having brought to light facts too little known by the general public and particularly by the English-speaking community.
Consequently, the Chambre de Commerce submits, in the summary of its findings, that the decrease of the French Canadian representation in the civil service is due in part to the development of certain abuses in the civil service, more particularly the creation of powerful groups within the service and the failure to recognize official bilingualism; it therefore asksthat the powers of the Civil Service Commission be increased so as to prevent the natural creation of powerful groups in the public service from being an obstacle to the appointment of civil servants of French Canadian origin to high executive positions.
Secondly, it suggests that bilingualism be officially recognized in the service.
The act of 1919 establishing the charter of the Canadian civil service did not take into account the requirements of official bilingualism.
Through this error, the classification of civil servants is a source of serious injustice and disagreement. The case submitted by the Chambre de Commerce will illustrate that fact. The bilingual typist and stenographer are both in the same class as the unilingual typist and stenographer. They draw the same salary although they are required to know two languages instead of one. Often the bilingual stenographer is called upon to do translation work in spite of the fact that she is supposed to be qualified only to take shorthand in both languages. She is thus expected to do the job of a translator although she is not paid as such.
More than ever, and I expect the situation will grow worse, the federal government intervenes in the affairs of the private citizen. More than ever the French Canadian people must keep in touch with the various departments. Every day the government

must deal with the French Canadian citizens on matters related to taxation, to import permits, to rationing, to unemployment insurance or to family allowances. I wish the government would always do it in French in order to avoid much trouble and much discrimination.
